title: Orthogonal Projections
short: Find the closest point in a subspace.
trouble: Students project onto a non-orthogonal basis one vector at a time and add.

blocks.html: What is the closest point of a subspace to a given vector? In the plane, drop a perpendicular. In any dimension, the answer is the orthogonal projection, and it rests on the splitting $\mathbb{R}^n = W \oplus W^{\perp}$ from orthogonal complements and on a basis of $W$.

Onto a line. The projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the line through $\mathbf{u}$ is $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u},$$ and $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ (check: $\mathbf{z}\cdot\mathbf{u}$ $= \mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u} - \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}$ $= 0$).

If $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_p\}$ is an orthogonal basis of $W$, the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $W$ is $$\role[projection onto W]{output}{\hat{\mathbf{y}}} = \role[weight for u1]{coefficient}{\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_1}}\role[basis vector]{vector}{\mathbf{u}_1} + \cdots + \frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_p}{\mathbf{u}_p\cdot\mathbf{u}_p}\mathbf{u}_p.$$ Then $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is in $W^{\perp}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the point of $W$ closest to $\mathbf{y}$.

Why closest? Take any $\mathbf{v}$ in $W$. Then $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}$ $= (\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}) + (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{v})$. The first piece is in $W^{\perp}$ and the second is in $W$, so they are orthogonal and the Pythagorean theorem gives $\lVert\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$ $= \lVert\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\rVert^{2} + \lVert\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}$. That is smallest exactly when $\mathbf{v} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}$. And why does the formula give a vector with $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ in $W^{\perp}$? Dot $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ with $\mathbf{u}_1$: because $\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_j = 0$ for $j \neq 1$, only the first term of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ survives, and it cancels $\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_1$ exactly.

blocks.title: Projection onto a plane
blocks.q: Project $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$ onto $W = \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2\}$ with $\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$, and find the distance from $\mathbf{y}$ to $W$.
steps: First check the basis is orthogonal: $\mathbf{u}_1\cdot\mathbf{u}_2 = -1 + 1 + 0 = 0$. ✓

blocks.name: la-proj
blocks.cap: The projection $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ lies in the plane $W$; the leftover $\mathbf{z}$ meets $W$ at a right angle. Turn the picture and edit $\mathbf{y}$.

blocks.html: Projecting onto each vector of a non-orthogonal basis and adding. The formula above needs an orthogonal basis; with a slanted basis the pieces overlap and the sum overshoots. Example: $W$ = the $xy$-plane with basis $(1, 0, 0)$, $(1, 1, 0)$ and $\mathbf{y} = (0, 2, 1)$. The true projection is $(0, 2, 0)$, but the separate projections are $(0, 0, 0)$ and $(1, 1, 0)$, which add to $(1, 1, 0)$: wrong. Fix it by making the basis orthogonal first (Gram–Schmidt) or by solving the normal equations of least squares. Check: $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$ must be orthogonal to every basis vector.

blocks.name: la-proj
blocks.cap: Press "Add the separate projections" to see the wrong answer; then "Make the basis orthogonal" and press it again: now the two agree.

blocks.html: With an orthonormal basis (orthogonal unit vectors) as the columns of $U$, the formula becomes $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = UU^{T}\mathbf{y}$: the matrix $UU^{T}$ is the projection matrix onto $W$.
